row.overview: A little-visited summit on the Cascade Crest near Stevens Pass, WA. Spinnaker Peak rises above the headwaters of the Tye River between Lichtenberg Mountain and Tye Peak, about a mile from the Pacific Crest Trail. It's rarely climbed, largely because the surrounding terrain is a thick, brushy bushwhack once snow melts out; most parties instead treat it as an off-trail winter or spring snow climb, often paired with neighboring Martin Peak.
row.beta: Two options exist to reach Spinnaker Peak's summit: the easier line climbs directly to the col between Point 5261 and Spinnaker Peak (steepest section of the trip, but low-exposure on the right line, and an ice axe isn't required if only Spinnaker is the objective); the harder option climbs Point 5261 first and follows the narrow, steeply-dropping ridge to Spinnaker's summit, which does require an ice axe and should be avoided in higher avalanche danger. The peak is seldom climbed despite its proximity to US Highway 2.
row.turnaround: Because this is an off-trail, unmarked route in avalanche and whiteout-prone terrain, set a turnaround time before starting and stick to it if visibility drops, the narrow ridge/col ices up, or avalanche conditions deteriorate — don't press on toward the summit once conditions no longer match what was planned for.

row.pro_needs: None. The route is non-technical; an ice axe is not required for Spinnaker alone, though many parties carry one for general snow travel or the connecting slopes to Martin Peak.
row.best_season: Best climbed roughly December through April on a consolidated snowpack, when the brush and loose talus that otherwise cover this route are buried; spring (Mar-May) often gives the most reliable travel with corn-snow conditions. A summer ascent is explicitly not recommended by trip reports — thick vegetation and off-trail bushwhacking make the same line a slog once the snow is gone. Always check the NWAC Stevens Pass zone forecast before going, since both the approach basin and the nearby PCT corridor cross avalanche terrain.
row.approach: Park at the Yodelin lot on US 2 (the former Yodelin ski area's lot, now used for overflow parking, roughly 1.7 miles from the Stevens Pass Ski Area pedestrian overpass, around milepost 60). Cross the highway and follow the old ski-area road south into the valley, staying near Nason Creek where crossings/snow bridges are most reliable, then continue into the open basin below the Spinnaker-Tye Peak ridge before turning up to the gap below Point 5261.
row.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line back through the gap and down into the basin to the Nason Creek valley and the Yodelin lot. With a stable, consolidated snowpack the open basin can offer a quick glissade or snowshoe/ski descent, but avoid dropping onto the Pacific Crest Trail tread itself for winter travel — it crosses several avalanche paths near here.
row.bail: Retreat down the south slopes is possible from most points.

days.note: From the Yodelin lot on US 2 (~3,600 ft), bushwhack down to and across Nason Creek (a snow bridge or log crossing is typical in winter/spring), then climb into the open basin between Tye Peak and the Spinnaker-Martin ridge. Ascend the basin's north side at a sustained ~35-degree angle to gain the ridge, then follow it to the Spinnaker summit; most parties add the ~10-minute round-trip side jaunt to Martin Peak. This is predominantly a winter/spring snow climb — summer condition is described as a rough, thick bushwhack, so nearly all reported ascents happen on a firm snowpack with snowshoes/traction and an ice axe rather than in bare-ground summer conditions.

approach_variants.name: Nason Creek basin to the Point 5261 col
approach_variants.notes: Park in the overflow lot off US-2 a couple of miles east of the ski area, cross the highway on foot and pick up the old ski-area access road into the valley, keeping near the creek where crossings and snow bridges are most reliable. Continue into the open basin below the Spinnaker-Tye ridge before turning up toward the gap. Almost every ascent is made on winter or spring snowpack; once the snow is gone this is a thick, unpleasant bushwhack that parties generally avoid, so the season is short and conditions-driven rather than weather-driven.
hazards: Avalanche terrain in the approach basin and in the nearby chutes
A narrow, corniced connecting ridge on the harder variant
No maintained trail and rarely a boot-packed track
Thick devil's club and brush once the snow melts out
Windblown snow that ices the sub-summit ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the climb is the col between Point 5261 and Spinnaker Peak. Coming up out of the basin, Point 5261 is the nearer rocky sub-summit and Spinnaker the higher point beyond it; the col is the low saddle between the two, and the ground rising out of it is the steepest of the whole trip although on a well-chosen line it carries little exposure and needs no axe if Spinnaker is your only objective. Take the col directly. The alternative — climbing Point 5261 first and following the connecting ridge across — is a materially different proposition: that crest is narrow, drops steeply into a series of small notches, ices over when windblown, wants an ice axe, and should be left alone with any avalanche danger about. So the check is simple: if you find yourself on a knife-edged crest with cornices and notches, you have taken the harder variant rather than the standard one, and the col is below and to your side. On the way down, keep off the trail tread itself for winter travel, since it crosses several avalanche paths near here.

bivy.name: The basin between Tye Peak and Spinnaker Peak
bivy.notes: A genuine winter camp rather than a summer one, and the natural base for Spinnaker Peak and its neighbour Martin Peak at the head of the Tye. The approach is from US 2 about two miles east of Stevens Pass, on the old road serving the Yodelin area, then up into the drainage on snowshoes or skis; the round trip to Spinnaker is around eight miles with a top out near 5,600 feet. From the basin the usual line traverses the northeast ridge past a subsidiary point around 5,300 feet, occasionally dropping onto the south side to avoid rock before regaining the crest. Parties combining Spinnaker with Tye Peak use this basin as the link between the two, which is the main argument for camping in it rather than doing either as a day trip. Everything here depends on snow cover — in summer the same ground is a slow thrash through slide alder and the peaks are seldom visited. Avalanche assessment is not optional; these are open, wind-loaded, lee slopes below a ridge crest, and the terrain traps in the drainage are real.
bivy.water: Melted snow in winter. In late summer the basin holds little or nothing reliable — carry what you need.
bivy.permit: National forest, no permit, no quota. Access from the highway east of the pass is across a mix of ownership near the old Yodelin development, so park on public ground and read the signs rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Open snow basin in winter, holding as many parties as care to spread out. In summer it is brush and boulder with very little usable flat ground.

row.overview: The Sitkum Glacier is the standard route on Glacier Peak — the most remote of Washington's major volcanoes. There's no technical crux, but the climb is defined by its long wilderness approach: many miles of trail just to reach a high camp, deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It's a true backcountry expedition rewarded by solitude and a wild summit.
row.beta: From Boulder Basin (5,500-6,000 ft), traverse SE onto the Sitkum Glacier and ascend a corridor on its left (climber's) side heading NE toward a saddle near 9,500 ft by Sitkum Spire. From the saddle, follow the pumice ridge toward the summit, staying right of and below the peak, then finish up a snow chute to the top. Crevasse danger is generally minimal and the route rarely steepens significantly.
row.turnaround: Turn around by early afternoon on summit day; the long descent to a remote camp leaves no margin for late finishes.
row.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at many trailheads.
row.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Glacier Peak Wilderness; the approach is 9+ trail miles from the nearest paved road. A satellite messenger (inReach/SPOT) is recommended.
row.descent: Reverse the route to Boulder Basin camp and the long trail out.

row.pro_needs: Glacier protection only — pickets for the steeper upper snow and crevasse zones.
row.best_season: Late June through August — snow-covered glacier, melted-out approach trails. Earlier means deep snow on the long approach; later opens crevasses and bares loose rock.
row.approach: The White Chuck approach described below is effectively gone: White Chuck River Trail #643 has been listed as inaccessible since the 2003 flood, and the White Chuck Road (FR 23) is closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7, about 5 miles of old roadbed short of the old trailhead, beyond which the valley is unmaintained travel with a river ford. Parties now come in from the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead instead, climbing to the Pacific Crest Trail at White Pass and following it north over Red Pass to the Sitkum Creek junction. From the White Chuck River Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of White Chuck River Road/FR 23), follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) upstream through old-growth forest. The trail fords/bridges several tributaries — Pumice Creek, Glacier Creek, and Kennedy Creek — which serve as reliable water sources but can run high with snowmelt in early summer. At about 5.5 miles reach the former Kennedy Hot Springs/Kennedy Guard Station area (~3,300 ft) — still a popular campsite, but the historic hot-springs pool, lodge, and guard station were destroyed and buried by the October 2003 flood/debris flow and were never rebuilt; there is no usable hot pool here. Continue roughly 1.5 miles farther to Sitkum Creek and the junction with the Pacific Crest Trail (~3,850 ft). Turn north (left) on the PCT for about a half mile to a forested campsite near 4,100 ft — a common lower camp. From there, leave the maintained trail and follow a steep, unmaintained climbers' path (locally described as 'more like a fisherman's route than a trail') straight up the forested ridge to Boulder Basin (5,500–6,000 ft), where the trees break and the standard high camp sits on heather/rock benches with running water nearby. From camp, ascend snowfields southeast/uphill onto the toe of the Sitkum Glacier. Note: the White Chuck River Road and Trail sustained major washout damage in the October 2003 floods and has had repeated closures/repairs since — confirm current road-end and trail status with the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest before relying on this approach, as in bad years the effective trailhead moves miles downstream.
row.descent_text: This is a walk-off/glacier descent with no rappelling — reverse the ascent line. From the summit, descend the pumice Sitkum ridge back to the ~9,500 ft saddle east of Sitkum Spire, then descend the Sitkum Glacier's upper section, staying in the corridor left of the icefall/rock rib that splits the glacier's lower half, back down to Boulder Basin. Crevasses exist on the Sitkum but are sparse and generally avoidable with standard route-finding; a rope, harness, and a few pickets are still standard kit. From Boulder Basin, follow the steep climbers' path back down to the PCT/White Chuck Trail junction and retrace the White Chuck River Trail to the trailhead.
row.bail: Boulder Basin (or your high camp) is the bail point; from the upper mountain you retreat to camp. Given the remoteness, there is no quick escape — bailing means the same long walk out.

pitch_detail.notes: Follow the White Chuck River Trail about 5.5 miles to the old Kennedy Hot Springs site, then 1.5 miles more to Sitkum Creek and the PCT. Go north on the PCT about half a mile to a forest camp near 4,100 ft, then take the steep, unmaintained climbers' path up the ridge south of Sitkum Creek to Boulder Basin (5,500–6,000 ft), the usual high camp. Confirm road and trail status before going.

From Boulder Basin, head southeast up snowfields, or a climbers' path later in the season, into a wide snow bowl below the glacier. Do not take the left-hand moraine. It leads to an awkward traverse under a wall of loose rock and then across a steep snowfield to get back on line. Scout the entry the evening before if arriving late, and rope up where the snow meets the ice.

Climb slightly south to the corridor beside the rock feature that splits the lower glacier, then trend northeast. Above that gap the angle eases. Aim for the saddle near 9,500 ft just east of Sitkum Spire, the obvious rock finger on the west summit ridge. Crevasses are not abundant but include hidden ones, even low down, and late season turns stretches to bare ice. Leave camp early, before the snow softens.

From the saddle, follow the pumice ridge toward the summit block. The footing is loose and tiring with no technical difficulty, and most parties unrope here. The saddle can be icy or rimed early in the day, so keep crampons handy. Note where you left the glacier: finding that spot again in a whiteout is the key to the descent.

Keep right of and slightly below the summit, traversing pumice or snow to one of several chutes that climb to the top on its right. The alternative turns left across the upper Scimitar Glacier, then climbs steeply right up the summit snow to the top. The summit gully can hold avalanche debris and a steep final headwall after storms. Descend the same way.

itinerary.cal: White Chuck River Road (FR 23) washout near mile 3.7-4 adds extra road-walking distance to this approach until repaired; best conditions are typically July-September.

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River Trail #643 (the historic standard)
approach_variants.notes:
This was the standard way up Glacier Peak and the road access has been unreliable for a very long time. The last several miles of FR 23 to the White Chuck trailhead have been reported blocked — at one point with large boulders placed at the turnoff — and reports of the road being driveable and undriveable have alternated over the years. Confirm with the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie forest before relying on it, because in a bad year the effective trailhead moves miles downstream.

From the trailhead at about 2,350 ft the trail runs upstream through old growth, crossing Pumice, Glacier and Kennedy Creeks — reliable water, but high with snowmelt in early summer. At about five and a half miles is the old Kennedy Hot Springs area at around 3,300 ft, still a popular campsite; the pool, lodge and guard station were destroyed by the 2003 flood and never rebuilt, so there is no usable hot pool there.

Another mile and a half brings you to Sitkum Creek and the PCT junction at about 3,850 ft. Turn north on the PCT for about half a mile to a forested camp near 4,100 ft.
hazards: unreliable road access to the trailhead over many years
creek fords running high with early-summer snowmelt
steep unmaintained climbers' path with no signage leaving the PCT
crevasses on the Sitkum
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The path that leaves the PCT for Boulder Basin is unsigned and steeper than anything before it — climbers describe it as more of a fisherman's track than a trail. The test is direction, not appearance: the correct path goes STRAIGHT UP the forested ridge. Anything that contours is the PCT or a game trail.

You know you have arrived at the top of it when the trees break: Boulder Basin at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft is heather and rock benches with running water, and it is the standard high camp. If you are still in continuous forest, you are below it, however long the climb has felt.

From camp the route ascends snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum. Rope up at the point the snowfield stops being a slope you can see the bottom of and becomes continuous glacier — there is no rock landmark for this, so the transition is judged on the ground rather than found.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk and the PCT (the reliable alternative)
approach_variants.notes: Because the White Chuck side has been unreliable for years, parties reach this side of the mountain instead from the North Fork Sauk River trailhead, climbing to White Pass on the PCT and then travelling north over Red Pass toward the Glacier Creek and Sitkum ground. It is substantially longer and is chosen for access rather than for the climbing.
hazards: very long approach on the PCT with substantial gain and loss
no signed junction for the climbers' path
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route above is unchanged: the marker is Boulder Basin — trees giving way to heather and rock benches with running water at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft — and then snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum above it. Arriving from the north on the PCT the risk is passing the drainage entirely, so identify the Sitkum Creek and Glacier Creek junctions on the map before you set out rather than expecting signage.

climbing_route.label: Snowfields onto the glacier toe
climbing_route.notes: From the Boulder Basin camp at 5,500-6,000 ft, head southeast up snowfields and moraine to gain the toe of the Sitkum Glacier. This is the one place parties routinely go wrong: taking the left-hand moraine commits you to an awkward traverse beneath a wall of loose rock and then across a steep snowfield to recover the correct line. Sort the entry out in daylight if you can, and rope up before stepping onto glacier ice.

climbing_route.label: Lower glacier corridor
climbing_route.notes: Trend slightly south to take the corridor on the left side of the rock feature that divides the lower glacier, then work back northeast. Both open and hidden crevasses are present here and the crossing points shift year to year and even week to week, so expect to weave and to reverse a line or two. Late-season melt-out exposes more bare ice and pushes the practical route further off any recorded track — a GPS trace from a previous party is a hint, not a route.

climbing_route.label: Upper glacier to the saddle
climbing_route.notes: Continue northeast up the upper glacier to a saddle at roughly 9,500 ft just east of Sitkum Spire. The firn line on the upper glacier has been retreating and bare ice is increasingly exposed, which makes crampons and a firmer belay standard rather than optional in late summer. A bergschrund sits below the saddle and is the last crevasse hazard on the ascent. This is a shaded, exposed slope late in the day — softening snow after mid-morning is the reason parties leave camp in the small hours.

climbing_route.label: Sitkum Ridge pumice
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle, leave the glacier for the pumice of Sitkum Ridge. This is loose, ball-bearing volcanic debris on a moderate slope — no technical difficulty, but tiring underfoot and easy to send rock down onto anyone behind. Most parties unrope here. Being off the glacier, it is also the point where a whiteout descent becomes hard to navigate by feel, so mark the spot where you leave the snow.

climbing_route.label: Summit slope
climbing_route.notes: Stay to the right of and slightly below the summit as you gain height, then take the snow chute that leads up to the top. The whole route is a glacier and snow climb with no rock pitches, but it is a long day at altitude on an isolated volcano where weather closes in quickly and the descent retraces every crevasse crossing made on the way up.

bivy.name: Boulder Basin
bivy.notes: The standard planned high camp, in an open meadow basin at the treeline with the glacier toe above. It is a pleasant place — flowers, waterfalls, and correspondingly aggressive marmots and bugs — but earning it means a long approach and then a steep, unmaintained climbers' path straight up a forested ridge with a full pack. It is about ten miles from the road end, and the road itself has a long history of washouts, so confirm where the trailhead actually is before you plan the day.
bivy.water: Waterfalls and snowmelt streams run through the basin; dependable into late summer but shrinking as the season goes on. Filter it
bivy.permit: No backcountry permit is required for overnight use in this wilderness
bivy.capacity: Several established sites on heather and rock benches at treeline, spread through the basin between roughly 5,500 and 6,000 ft

bivy.name: Kennedy Guard Station area
bivy.notes: The lowest planned stop, about 5.5 miles in and still widely used. Do not plan on soaking: the historic hot pool, lodge and guard station here were buried by the 2003 flood and debris flow and were never rebuilt. Useful as a first night for parties splitting the approach, or as a retreat in bad weather, but it is a long way and a lot of gain below the glacier.

bivy.name: Sitkum Creek / PCT junction camp
bivy.notes: A lower fallback for parties who run out of daylight on the long walk in, sitting where the climbers' path leaves the maintained trail. Below treeline, so it is sheltered and out of the weather, but it leaves the entire steep climbers' path plus 1,500 ft of gain before you are even at the standard camp.
bivy.capacity: A small forested site or two just north of the trail junction

row.name: Doorway Flake
row.fa: Bill Enger and Yale Lewis, June 19, 2019
hazards: Steep, brushy, poorly maintained approach with stream crossings and old rockslide/avalanche debris
Remote location extends any self-rescue or evacuation timeline
row.overview: A 5-pitch, 700-ft route on the Far Western Wall reaching a distinctive hanging flake, with sculpted-knob face climbing low down and a bolt-protected 5.9 face crux on pitch two.
row.beta: Pitch 1 (5.8) climbs sculpted knobs to a hanging flake with stemming and crack moves. Pitch 2 (5.9) is the crux — bolt-protected face climbing. Pitch 3 (5.7) follows a clean crack system, and pitches 4-5 (5.6) ease through dihedrals and slab to the top.
row.turnaround: There is no quick bail once on route above the 4th-class approach scramble; start early enough to finish the climb, rappel, and reverse the multi-hour approach before dark, and back off if thunderstorms threaten the exposed face pitch.
row.rappels: 5 raps on two 60m ropes to Fixe chain anchors
row.comms: No reliable cell coverage on the wall or approach; a satellite communicator is recommended.

waypoints.name: Squire Creek Trailhead (Trail #654, end of FS Rd 2040)
waypoints.directions: From I-5 take the Arlington exit and drive SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington. Leave town on Squire Creek Road and follow it to the washout gate, which is where the road ends for vehicles and where you park. Everything past the gate is walked, starting along the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing.

waypoints.name: Grassy saddle (South Face routes)
waypoints.note: Shares the same ~3 hr approach as the wall's other South Face routes.

timing.recommendedStart: A pre-dawn alpine start is advisable given the multi-hour approach and multi-pitch descent

row.detailed_rack: Single standard rack to 4 inches, about a dozen quickdraws (plus a few longer/extended ones), and two 60m ropes for the rappel descent.
what_to_bring: Approach shoes for a rough, 4 hr approach with a creek ford and 4th-class scrambling
pro_tips: The 4th-class approach traverse to the Far Western Wall is exposed — move carefully with packs on
Bring a topo; hand-drilled bolts can be hard to spot in shade
watch_out: Bolt-protected crux face pitch (2) — inspect conditions before committing
row.pro_needs: Bolt protection on the pitch-2 face crux, with gear placements in the flake, crack, and dihedral sections on the remaining pitches; all bolts are hand-drilled per Wilderness rules.
row.best_season: Best mid-summer through early fall (roughly July-September); the Boulder River Wilderness holds snow into July and can see new snow by October.
row.approach: South Face is another wall within the same Squire Creek Walls complex as Waterfall Basin, reached via the same Darrington-area approach: I-5 to the Arlington exit, SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, then Squire Creek Road to the washout-blocked parking area. From there, follow the same rough, unmaintained approach — the old roadbed past a landslide crossing, a faint trail through streambed and alder brush, a ford of Squire Creek, and obscure forest track — before breaking into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car; South Face is one of the walls encountered within that same basin complex, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
row.descent_text: Rappel the line of ascent using the fixed hand-drilled bolt and Fixe chain anchors; two 60m ropes recommended.
row.bail: Descent is by rappelling the route itself from the nearest fixed anchor — there is no separate walk-off.

pitch_detail.notes: The namesake flake sits about 6 m above the talus at the nearest point of the far western wall. Boulder up sculpted knobs to the flake's lower edge, where a good crack takes a range of sizes, and stem over the lip. A 4-inch cam in the top of the flake protects knobs to a bolt; step right up cracks and ledges past another bolt, then back left via a quartz-studded block to a big ledge and smear past two bolts to the anchor.

From the right end of the ledge, face moves lead right to a visible bolt. Easy ground reaches a steep block protected by a 1.5-inch horizontal, then a vertical edge that faces right, then left past an alcove, with four bolts: sustained, fun 5.9 face climbing. Step down left to a narrow ledge and a high bolt, undercling out left to a diving-board feature (3/4-inch gear), and climb its dihedral past one bolt.

Go left off the ledge up edges with a slot for gear and a bolt, then straight up to a large ring of bushes and pass it on the left. Reach left on smears into a clean crack system through the White Spot, pass a hanging block with a white stump on its left, move right to a 1-inch crack, and traverse right into an easy trough to the anchor.

Cruise up easy dihedrals including a long 4-inch layback crack. Where it turns right, step left for gear or pad up to a single bolt at a stance under a patch of bushes, then smear up and right near the hanging branches and move left past them to the anchor.
One bolt protects a slabby hump heading straight for the summit; scramble the blocks above to a chain anchor. Descent is by rappelling the route with two ropes.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through mid-September, when the Squire Creek ford is low and the slabs dry out between rains

July.reason: The creek drops and the south-facing slab dries; heat on the sunny wall can make afternoon friction greasy.

June.reason: Snowmelt keeps Squire Creek high for the ford, the slabs seep after rain, and snow can linger in the basin into early summer.

August.reason: Lowest water at the ford and the driest rock of the year; start early to climb before the sun makes the slab hot.

October.reason: Autumn rain on this very wet west slope keeps the rock damp, days are short, and new snow is possible in the basin.

September.reason: Cooler temperatures give better friction on the sunny slab, though the first fall rains leave the rock wet for a day or two.

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Squire Creek Road out of Darrington to the washout gate, then the old roadbed on foot past the flagged landslide crossing.

Turn right at the two cut logs with old logging cable onto the well-beaten boot track. Ford the creek, climb steeply through old-growth forest — the upper section is steep and dirty — and break out into grassland at the grassy saddle bivy, roughly three hours from the trailhead. A second, smaller saddle lies ten minutes west along the wall.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek
Steep dirty forest on the upper boot track
approach_variants.baseFinding: The main grassy saddle, at the start of Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer, is the reference point for the whole South Face; the smaller saddle further west is not it. From the saddle the grey granite apron runs out below the wall and the lines are picked off it. Rock here is generally clean slab with cracks that can be dirt-filled low down — dirty cracks near the ground are normal on this face and are not evidence you are off route. The sources consulted give no ground-level marker unique to this line, so identify it off the wall topo from the saddle rather than from anything underfoot.

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.

bivy.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
bivy.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
bivy.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need

row.name: Skeena26
row.fa: David Whitelaw, Bill Enger, and Yale Lewis, September 17, 2012
hazards: Steep, brushy, poorly maintained approach with a creek ford and old rockslide/avalanche debris
Remote location extends any self-rescue or evacuation timeline
row.overview: A 12-pitch, 1,500-ft friction climb on immaculate, knobby grey granite, with a polished 5.9 crux on pitch one easing into mostly 5.4-5.6 climbing above, finishing on clean splitter cracks overlooking Whitehorse Mountain.
row.beta: Pitch 1 climbs a narrow 'whale's back' of stone between facing corners on polished friction, protected by nine bolts, and holds the route's crux. Subsequent pitches ease to 5.4-5.6 with occasional 5.8 sections. The final pitch features clean splitter cracks (5.7) finishing on the buttress crest with views over Whitehorse Mountain.
row.turnaround: With 12 pitches and a multi-hour approach, treat this as a full-day objective with no quick bail; start early enough to finish and hike out before dark, and back off if water/seepage or building weather make the polished friction pitches unsafe.
row.rappels: Rappel the route on 50m ropes (most pitches take a full 50m); pitches 5-6 can be combined using 60m ropes
row.comms: No reliable cell coverage on the wall or approach; a satellite communicator is recommended.

row.pro_needs: Bolt-protected on the polished pitch-1 crux (9 bolts) and other friction sections, with natural gear placements filling in on lower-angle pitches and the final splitter-crack pitch.
row.best_season: Best from mid-summer through early fall (roughly July-September); parties note lingering water/seepage on pitch 7 even in-season, and the Boulder River Wilderness holds snow at elevation into July.
row.approach: South Face is another wall within the same Squire Creek Walls complex as Waterfall Basin, reached via the same Darrington-area approach: I-5 to the Arlington exit, SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, then Squire Creek Road to the washout-blocked parking area. From there, follow the same rough, unmaintained approach — the old roadbed past a landslide crossing, a faint trail through streambed and alder brush, a ford of Squire Creek, and obscure forest track — before breaking into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car; South Face is one of the walls encountered within that same basin complex, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
row.descent_text: Rappel the line of ascent; 50-meter ropes are adequate for most pitches, while 60-meter ropes allow combining pitches 5 and 6 to speed the descent.
row.bail: Retreat is by rappelling the route from the nearest fixed anchor — no separate walk-off exists.

pitch_detail.notes: Find the narrow whale's-back rib between two facing corners; the nine bolts are hard to see in the shade. A bouldery 5.9 move gains the rib, then 5.7-5.8 friction leads to polished rock near the top with a few more 5.9 moves. Step onto a flake on the left, place gear in good cracks just above, then traverse right to the belay ledge.

The character of most of the route: friction on brilliant white granite covered in knobs and bumps, mostly 5.4-5.6. Bolts are spaced roughly 10-20 feet apart and hard to spot in shade, so look ahead before leaving each anchor.
More knobbed slab at 5.6 with occasional 5.8 moves. On rappel, 60 m ropes let these two pitches be combined into one rappel.
A 5.8 section starts on this pitch, and it can carry running water even when the rest of the route is dry. Be ready for wet smears on this pitch.
There is a gear crack on this pitch that is easy to miss; climbing past it turns the pitch into a long runout. Look for it before running it out.

Climb up and right past four bolts (nothing harder than 5.7), then finish on clean 5.7 splitter cracks and a few face moves past the left side of an overhang, onto the forested ledge on top of the buttress with views of Whitehorse Mountain. The wall's true summit is further up brushy scrambling.

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek washout to the west saddle
approach_variants.notes: Drive Squire Creek Road out of Darrington until the washout blocks it and park at the gate. Follow the old roadbed past the landslide crossing, watching for two cut logs on either side of the road with old logging cable visible, where a well-established boot track drops right toward the creek. Ford Squire Creek at its shallowest point, follow the climbers' track upstream across a tributary, then climb through two gullies on steep, muddy tread until the ground opens at the grassy saddle below the wall.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn, once the Squire Creek ford has dropped; the wall itself faces south-southwest and takes direct sun only through the middle of the day
hazards: The Squire Creek ford is difficult in early season
Faint, flagged approach track through alder and streambed with several places to lose it
The bolts on the first pitch are old and hard to see against the pale stone
approach_variants.baseFinding: The grassy saddle where the climbers' path tops out is NOT the start of this route — that is where the other lines on this wall begin, and stopping there is the commonest mistake. From the saddle keep going LEFT, west, along the base of the wall for five to ten minutes to a second and smaller saddle, then scramble up grass into a minor gully. The proof is the first pitch itself: it climbs a narrow whale's back of stone, a rounded rib of clean grey-white granite standing proud between two facing corners of much more broken rock, with a line of bolts up it. Those bolts are old and hard to pick out against the pale stone, so identify the rib shape first and the hardware second. If you are on broken, cornered rock rather than a smooth rounded rib, you are in one of the flanking corners and not on the route. If the main grassy saddle is still below and to your right, you have not walked far enough west.

bivy.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges

This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.

row.overview: Marvin's Ear climbs the skyline ridge of Vega Tower — the sub-summit just east of Vega North Tower/Eros Tower — via a fully bolted 800-ft, 7-pitch alpine sport line (Grade III, 5.10b) through hard metaconglomerate rock. It was the first technical route up Vega Tower's west ridge proper (the only prior technical line, Starshot Ridge 5.8, was established in 1981 on a different aspect); climbing gets progressively more exposed as it skirts over the north face in the upper pitches.
row.beta: 800 feet, Grade III 5.10b, with well-protected cruxes though bolts are spaced further apart on easier (5.9-and-under) terrain. Prior to this route, only one other technical line (Starshot Ridge, 5.8, established 1981) existed on Vega Tower, and the west ridge itself was unclimbed until 2016/2017.

row.pro_needs: Fully bolted; quickdraws and a few alpine draws cover the whole route. A 70m rope is needed both to climb the longer pitches and to rappel.
row.approach: Same Sunrise Mine Trail approach as Mile High Club and Beyond Redlining: follow the trail roughly 2.5 miles to the last major switchback at about 4,300 ft, then leave the trail for a cairned talus traverse heading northeast across two talus fields toward the Vega towers (shared with the other Vega North Tower routes). Where the traverse for Mile High Club and Beyond Redlining continues toward the base of the main west face, Marvin's Ear branches off into a gully to the right (east) of Vega North Tower. Follow this gully up through cedar and heather — vegetated, sometimes loose ground — to a notch on the skyline ridge. From the notch, the last bit to the pitch-one belay involves loose 3rd-class terrain with some exposed 4th-class moves, landing on a grassy ledge that serves as the first belay. Because this gully approach is steeper and more vegetated than the open talus used by Mile High Club, expect a slower, more route-finding-dependent final approach, and be cautious of loose blocks in the gully, especially with parties above.
row.descent_text: Marvin's Ear is rappelled back down its own line (not via Mile High Club). Bolted anchors are set roughly 30m apart along the route, so a single 60m rope will come up short in places — bring a 70m rope, which lets you link some of the 30m-spaced stations into longer raps and reduces the rappel count to roughly four full-length raps rather than seven pitch-by-pitch rappels. Beta from parties who've done the descent numbers them R1 through R4: R1 has notable rope friction on the pull; R2 requires looking right near the end of the rope to find the next station; R3 trends straight down; R4 is straightforward. One notable trap: partway down you'll see a shiny pair of rap chains that looks like the anchor — it isn't the one to use. Instead traverse left to find a hidden bolt behind a rock, then continue left to the actual bolted rappel anchor (no chains), which is the correct line down. Watch for loose rock and rope-catching pinches throughout the descent, consistent with the route's overall character on this face.
row.bail: Any bolted anchor can serve as a bail point given the fully-bolted nature of the climb.

Bolts trend left toward the end of the pitch to reach the next belay.
The technical crux: a cruxy move over a bulge into another sustained, cruxy section; extend a few draws to manage rope drag.
A cool traverse left, then up through a fun corner to the anchor just below the summit.

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail, then the east-side gully
approach_variants.notes: Share the standard approach as far as the traverse: Sunrise Mine trailhead, two and a half miles of trail through the unbridged creek crossings to the LAST MAJOR SWITCHBACK before the pass zigzags, then the cairned northeast traverse across two talus fields. The difference comes at the end. Where the boot path for the other two routes carries on toward the open talus at the foot of the main west face, this one BRANCHES OFF into a gully on the RIGHT — the east side of the northern tower. The gully is steeper, more vegetated and slower than the open talus, and route-finding matters more on it than anywhere else on the approach.

approach_variants.baseFinding: Follow the gully on the east side of the tower up through CEDAR AND HEATHER — vegetation is the test, because the neighbouring routes' approach is bare talus and this one is not. The gully leads to a NOTCH ON THE SKYLINE RIDGE. From the notch, the last stretch is loose third-class with a few exposed fourth-class moves, landing on a GRASSY LEDGE that is the first belay. Confirm at the belay by looking up: the first bolt on this route is set notably HIGH above the stance and there are only about four bolts in the whole first rope length, so you scramble before you clip. Negative markers: if you are on open talus at the foot of the tower with two big boulders or a red gully in front of you, you never branched off and you are under the other tower's two routes; if you have found a single bolted belay on a narrow ledge past a lone fir, that is the arete route on the wrong tower.

bivy.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
